client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away six months ago from cancer. Everything just feels kind of gray and empty, like I go through the days but nothing really means anything anymore. I've also been pulling away from my friends, and honestly I'm not sure talking about it is going to change any of that, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you so much for being here and for giving this a try — that takes real courage, especially when things feel this heavy and uncertain. Losing your partner to cancer is an enormous loss, and what you're describing — that grayness, the sense of going through the motions, pulling back from people — those are deeply human responses to profound grief. I want you to know there's no pressure to feel hopeful about this process right away, and I'm genuinely glad you reached out. Can you tell me a little about what a typical day looks like for you right now?

client: A typical day is pretty much just... getting up because I have to, making coffee, going to work, coming home, and then sitting in the apartment until it's late enough to justify going to bed. I still sleep on my side of the bed, which is kind of embarrassing to admit, and the evenings are the worst because that's when we used to talk and just be together. I'm functioning, I guess, but it doesn't really feel like living.
therapist: Please don't be embarrassed about sleeping on your side of the bed — that's a tender, loving detail, not something to judge yourself for. What you're describing sounds like a kind of quiet, exhausting grief, where you're holding everything together on the outside but the evenings strip that away and remind you of exactly what's missing. I'm curious — when you're sitting in that apartment in the evenings, what kinds of thoughts tend to show up for you?

client: Mostly I think about things I should have done differently, like whether I was present enough during the last few months or if I said everything I needed to say. There's this one night near the end where I got frustrated and snapped at them over something completely stupid, and I keep coming back to that over and over. I know logically it was just one moment, but it feels like it says something terrible about me as a person.
therapist: That moment you keep returning to sounds like it's carrying so much weight — and it makes sense that your mind keeps going back there, because grief often searches for something to hold onto, even if what it finds is painful. But I want to gently offer this: one moment of frustration in the middle of an incredibly hard, exhausting time doesn't define the entirety of who you were to your partner, and it sounds like a very human response to an almost unbearable situation. What do you think your partner would say if they could see how much that moment is still haunting you?

client: Honestly, they probably would have told me to stop being so hard on myself, that's just the kind of person they were. But when I try to actually believe that, it feels like I'm just letting myself off the hook, like I'm using their kindness to excuse something that genuinely hurt them. So even though I can kind of see the logic in what you're saying, it doesn't really land emotionally, if that makes sense.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and it's actually a really important distinction you're making — knowing something intellectually and truly feeling it are two very different things, and grief can make that gap feel enormous. What strikes me is that you're essentially rejecting your partner's own perspective on you, the perspective of the person who knew you most intimately, because you don't feel you deserve their grace — and I wonder if that's worth sitting with for a moment. What do you think it would mean about you *as a person* if you did allow yourself to accept their forgiveness?

client: I think it would mean I have to accept that the relationship was good, that I was good enough, and then I'd have to fully face the fact that it's just... gone. Like the guilt is almost easier to hold onto because it gives me something to do with all this pain, something to fix or punish myself for. If I let that go, I'm not sure what's left except the loss itself.
therapist: What you just said is incredibly profound and self-aware — you've named something that many people never quite see in themselves, that the guilt has actually been serving a purpose, protecting you from the full weight of the loss underneath it. That kind of pain makes a lot of sense, because facing "it's gone and it was good" is in some ways harder than "it's gone and I failed," because there's nothing to fix, just something to grieve. I'm wondering — what feels most scary to you about sitting with the loss itself, without the guilt to hold onto?

client: I think what scares me most is that if I just grieve it purely, it feels like I'm moving toward eventually being okay, and being okay feels like a betrayal somehow, like I'm leaving them behind. There's a part of me that thinks staying in this pain is the last way I have of honoring how much they mattered. I don't know how to grieve someone without it feeling like I'm slowly erasing them.
therapist: What you're describing is one of the most tender and painful paradoxes of grief — the fear that healing is a kind of forgetting, that joy could somehow diminish what you had. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if carrying them forward doesn't mean staying in pain, but instead means letting the love itself, not the suffering, be what keeps them present in your life? What do you think your partner would want to be remembered *as* — the source of your ongoing pain, or something else?

client: They would have hated the idea of being the reason I'm suffering, I know that. But even as I say that, I'm not sure I know how to actually make that switch in practice, like how do you just decide to let love be the thing instead of pain when they're so tangled up together right now. It sounds right when you say it, but I don't really know what that would look like in my actual daily life.
therapist: You don't have to make that switch all at once — and honestly, expecting yourself to is probably too much to ask right now, when the loss is still so fresh and the love and pain are genuinely intertwined. In CBT we often start small and concrete, so I'm curious: are there any tiny moments in your day — a song they loved, a place you went together, something that makes you think of them — that feel more like warmth than like pain, even just briefly? That might be a place to start looking for what "love instead of suffering" could actually feel like in practice.

client: There is this one thing, actually — they used to make this really specific playlist for Sunday mornings, and sometimes when I'm making coffee I'll hear one of those songs on shuffle and for just a second it feels more like they're nearby than like they're gone. But then it shifts really quickly into this wave of sadness, so I've actually been avoiding music altogether because I don't trust myself to stay in that brief warm moment before it turns. I'm not sure I have enough control over where it takes me to try leaning into it on purpose.
therapist: That brief moment with the coffee and the song — that's actually really significant, because it tells you that the warmth is still there, that your connection to them hasn't disappeared, even if it gets quickly swept away by the grief. It makes complete sense that you've been protecting yourself by avoiding music, and that's not weakness — but I wonder if rather than trying to "stay in" that moment or control where it goes, the goal could simply be to notice it without immediately needing to escape it, almost like learning to trust yourself to feel it without being destroyed by it. What do you think would feel like a small enough, safe enough step — maybe even just one song, at a moment when you feel slightly steadier — that might let you experiment with that?

client: I think maybe one song could be manageable, but I'm worried about timing it right because there's no real moment in my week that feels "steady" anymore, they all kind of blur together with this underlying heaviness. And I guess I'm also a little afraid that if I do it intentionally, like as an exercise, it'll feel forced and clinical and ruin the naturalness of those accidental moments that have actually felt okay. I don't want to turn the one thing that's still giving me a small connection to them into something that feels like therapy homework.
therapist: That's such a valid and thoughtful concern, and I want to honor it — the last thing we want to do is turn something sacred into a checkbox. So let's set aside the idea of intentional exercises entirely, and instead just notice together that those accidental moments are already happening, already working in some small way, even within all the heaviness. What if the only "homework" was simply not avoiding music anymore — not seeking it out, not timing anything, just leaving the door open for those moments to find you the way they already have been? How does that feel compared to the more structured version?

client: That does feel less threatening, like there's not as much pressure attached to it. I think I could probably manage just not actively avoiding it, that feels more like removing a barrier than adding a task. I'm still a little nervous about the evenings specifically because that's when I'm most vulnerable, but maybe I don't have to figure all of that out right now.
therapist: It sounds like something shifted just a little there — a small but real sense of "I can do this one thing," and that matters. You're also showing a lot of wisdom in recognizing that the evenings are their own separate challenge that doesn't need to be solved today, and that's not avoidance, that's good pacing. As we wrap up for today, I'm curious — what's one thing from our conversation that you might carry with you this week, even just as something to sit with?
